To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The use of municipal accounting practices is significantly related to the level of political competition in the municipality, but the relation between the use of accounting practices and political competition is not monotonic; and the relation between the level of political accountability of the municipality and the use of municipal accounting is not monotonic.

(1) elected officials are more likely to disclose their actions if they are in a competitive political market; and (2) elected officials are less likely to disclose their activities if they have been in office for a longer period of time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of political competition on the incentives to use accounting and auditing practices in political markets.
the role of accounting in the political marketplace and with the implications of this role for accounting theory.
how the political marketplace influences the use of accounting and auditing by elected officials, and how the use of these practices in turn influences the marketplace.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the empirical evidence is consistent with the proposition that accounting and auditing practices are related to the degree of political competition, and that these practices are used by incumbents to signal to potential competitors their commitment to fiscal responsibility.
there is a positive relationship between political competition and the adoption of standard accounting and financial reporting practices.
the empirical results reported in the prior literature are consistent with the hypothesis that accounting and auditing practices are used by incumbents to influence the political marketplace.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the political competition model is a useful framework for evaluating the influence of accounting and auditing practices on political markets, but that the empirical results are mixed and require further study.
the use of accounting and auditing is not a substitute for the political market, but rather an important component in a political market.
the use of standard municipal accounting and auditing practices is associated with the degree of political competition in the market for elected office.
The main takeaway from our work is that
accounting and auditing practices are used to influence the political marketplace, not the constituents.
the use of accounting and auditing practices by elected officials may be more a product of political competition than a reflection of the preferences of constituents.
the use of accounting and auditing by local governments is not a random process.
